label: abbrev/no-swallows-a-sentence
text: The answer is no. It is denied.
claims: The answer is no. It is denied.
known_miss: "no" is in ABBREVIATIONS as the number abbreviation ("No. 5"), but it is also an extremely common English sentence-final word. R3 therefore refuses the break and fuses a refusal with whatever follows it — the worst possible pairing for a polarity-sensitive gate.

label: abbrev/fig-at-a-real-sentence-end
text: Refer to the fig. The next page follows.
claims: Refer to the fig. The next page follows.
known_miss: The dual of the Dr./p.m. tailoring UAX #29 leaves unresolved: an abbreviation that also ends a sentence cannot be told apart locally, so R3 always chooses no-break and fuses two sentences.

label: abbrev/inc-not-in-table

known_miss: "z.s.m." is left out of ABBREVIATIONS because it is clause-final as often as not; mid-sentence it therefore breaks and yields a fragment claim. A fragment fails the gate and is dropped (safe); a false merge would pass or fail two sentences together (unsafe).

label: digit/percent-then-stop

label: digit/ordered-list-marker
known_miss: An ordered-list marker is a digit followed by a full stop and a space, which R2 does not cover and R4 accepts, so the marker becomes its own claim. The gate then verifies the string "1." against a passage.

label: run/question
text: Is it approved? It is not.

label: run/bare-punctuation
known_miss: A terminator run with no words is still emitted as a claim. It carries no proposition, so the gate spends a verdict on punctuation.

label: r4/plain-pair
text: The contractor maintains insurance. The term is five years.

label: r4/quote-spans-the-boundary
known_miss: A closing quote is not whitespace, so R4 refuses the break and two sentences fuse. A quoted assertion and the narrator's sentence about it are then gated as one claim.

label: r4/parenthesis-spans-the-boundary
known_miss: Same defect through a closing paren: a parenthetical citation swallows the sentence after it.

label: r4/missing-space-after-stop
known_miss: R4's cost: a typo (or a PDF extraction that ate the space) fuses two sentences, and this is exactly what bad extraction produces.
